claim: Sexual activity and/or reproduction are associated with a doubling of life expectancy in the long-lived rodent genus Fukomys.
source: Sexual activity and/or reproduction are associated with a doubling of life expectancy in the long-lived rodent genus Fukomys.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data presented in Figure 1A showing breeders live significantly longer than non-breeders in both F. mechowii and F. micklemi

claim: Changes in the regulation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal stress axis play a key role regarding the extended life expectancy of reproductive vs. non-reproductive mole-rats.
source: This analysis suggests that changes in the regulation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal stress axis play a key role regarding the extended life expectancy of reproductive vs. non-reproductive mole-rats.
evidence: Based on analysis of 636 RNA-seq samples across 15 tissues showing differential expression in HPA axis components

claim: The up-regulation of the proteasome is linked with enhanced lifespan in Fukomys breeders.
source: In accordance with previous studies, the up-regulation of the proteasome and so-called 'anti-aging molecules', for example, dehydroepiandrosterone, is linked with enhanced lifespan.
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis showing proteasome up-regulation in breeders and citation to previous studies

claim: Up-regulation of dehydroepiandrosterone is linked with enhanced lifespan in Fukomys breeders.
source: In accordance with previous studies, the up-regulation of the proteasome and so-called 'anti-aging molecules', for example, dehydroepiandrosterone, is linked with enhanced lifespan.
evidence: Supported by down-regulation of SULT2A1 (which converts DHEA to inactive form) in breeders

claim: Up-regulation of the insulin-like growth factor 1/growth hormone axis is compatible with considerable lifespan prolongation in Fukomys.
source: For example, we found the up-regulation of the insulin-like growth factor 1/growth hormone axis and several other anabolic processes to be compatible with a considerable lifespan prolongation.
evidence: Based on differential expression data showing IGF1 and GH1 up-regulation in longer-lived breeders

claim: Findings from short-lived species cannot be fully transferred to longer-lived ones regarding aging mechanisms.
source: These contradictions question the extent to which findings from short-lived species can be transferred to longer-lived ones.
evidence: Based on contradictory findings where processes known to extend lifespan when inhibited in short-lived species are up-regulated in longer-lived Fukomys breeders

claim: Most current understanding of aging mechanisms comes from short-lived model species.
source: Most of our current understanding of the underlying mechanisms of aging comes from short-lived model species.
evidence: General statement about the state of aging research

claim: It is unclear to what extent insights from short-lived organisms can be transferred to long-lived species such as humans.
source: It is, however, still largely unclear to what extent insights obtained from short-lived organisms can be transferred to long-lived species, such as humans (Parker et al., 2004; Keller and Jemielity, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Parker et al., 2004 and Keller and Jemielity, 2006

claim: Studies involving organisms with particularly long lifespans have produced findings not always congruent with established aging theories.
source: Many studies that involved organisms with particularly long lifespans, for example, queens in social hymenoptera, birds, bats, African mole-rats, and primates, have produced findings that were not always congruent with established aging theories (Keller and Jemielity, 2006; Austad, 2009; Salmon et al., 2009; Austad, 2011; Dammann, 2017; Bens et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on long-lived organisms

claim: Fukomys families typically consist of 9-16 individuals.
source: These animals live in families (often called colonies) of usually consisting of 9–16 individuals (Sichilima et al., 2008; Šklíba et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Sichilima et al., 2008 and Šklíba et al., 2012

claim: An established Fukomys family typically consists of only one breeding pair and their progeny.
source: Regardless of group size, an established family typically consists of only one breeding pair (the founders of the family, often called king/queen) and their progeny from multiple litters (often called workers).
evidence: Description of Fukomys social structure

claim: Fukomys progeny do not engage in sexual activity in their natal family due to strict avoidance of incest.
source: Because of strict avoidance of incest (Burda, 1995), the progeny do not engage in sexual activity in the confines of their natal family, even after reaching sexual maturity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Burda, 1995

claim: Fukomys breeders reach the age of 20 years or more in captivity.
source: Interestingly, breeders reach the age of 20 years or more in captivity, whereas non-breeders usually die before their tenth birth date (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Fukomys non-breeders usually die before their tenth birth date in captivity.
source: Interestingly, breeders reach the age of 20 years or more in captivity, whereas non-breeders usually die before their tenth birth date (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The divergence of survival probabilities between breeders and non-breeders is found in all Fukomys species studied so far, irrespective of sex.
source: This divergence of survival probabilities between breeders and non-breeders is found in all Fukomys species studied so far, irrespective of sex.
evidence: General statement about pattern across Fukomys species

claim: No difference in diet or workload has been observed between breeders and non-breeders in captivity.
source: Because no difference in diet or workload has been observed between breeders and non-breeders in captivity, status-specific changes of gene expression after the transition from non-breeder to breeder are considered the most likely explanation of the differing lifespans (Dammann and Burda, 2006; Dammann et al., 2011).
evidence: Observation from captive studies cited to Dammann and Burda, 2006 and Dammann et al., 2011

claim: Status-specific changes of gene expression after the transition from non-breeder to breeder are considered the most likely explanation of the differing lifespans in Fukomys.
source: Because no difference in diet or workload has been observed between breeders and non-breeders in captivity, status-specific changes of gene expression after the transition from non-breeder to breeder are considered the most likely explanation of the differing lifespans (Dammann and Burda, 2006; Dammann et al., 2011).
evidence: Inference based on lack of other explanatory factors, supported by citations

claim: Markers of protein cross-linking and oxidation were higher in breeders of Ansell's mole-rats than in age-matched non-breeders.
source: Contrary to the predictions of both the advanced glycation formation theory (Morimoto and Cuervo, 2009) and the oxidative stress theory of aging (Harman, 1956; Harman, 2001), markers of protein cross-linking and -oxidation were surprisingly higher in breeders of Ansell's mole-rats (Fukomys anselli) than in age-matched non-breeders (Dammann et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dammann et al., 2012

claim: In Damaraland mole-rats, oxidative damage to proteins and lipids was significantly lower in breeding females than in their non-reproductive counterparts.
source: On the other hand, in the Damaraland mole-rat (Fukomys damarensis), oxidative damage to proteins and lipids was significantly lower in breeding females than in their non-reproductive counterparts (Schmidt et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2014

claim: Levels of unbound T4 (fT4) do not explain the intraspecific longevity differences between F. anselli breeders and non-breeders.
source: Still, nonetheless the levels of unbound T4 (fT4) do not explain the intraspecific longevity differences between F. anselli breeders and non-breeders because the levels of this hormone did not differ between the two cohorts (Henning et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Henning et al., 2014

claim: Non-breeding giant mole-rats maintain fairly stable gene expression into relative old ages, in contrast to the shorter-lived Norway rat.
source: Closely connected to the topic of this paper is the finding that non-breeding giant mole-rats (Fukomys mechowii) maintain fairly stable gene expression into relative old ages, quite in contrast to the shorter-lived Norway rat (Sahm et al., 2018a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sahm et al., 2018a

claim: Naked mole-rats tended globally to show opposite changes in the transition from non-breeders to breeders compared to shorter-lived guinea pigs.
source: Interestingly, a recent study by Bens et al., 2018 found that the longest-lived rodent, the naked mole-rat Heterocephalus glaber, tended globally to show opposite changes in the transition from non-breeders to breeders compared to shorter-lived guinea pigs.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bens et al., 2018

claim: Naked mole-rat non-breeders have been reported to be as long-lived as breeders.
source: until very recently, naked mole-rat non-breeders have been reported to be as long-lived as breeders (Sherman and Jarvis, 2002; Buffenstein, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sherman and Jarvis, 2002 and Buffenstein, 2008

claim: A lifespan advantage of breeders over non-breeders was reported in female naked mole-rats but not males in 2018.
source: In 2018, a lifespan advantage of breeders over non-breeders was reported in females (but not males), yet the divergence of the two groups appeared to be considerably smaller than in Fukomys (Ruby et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruby et al., 2018

claim: Both Fukomys and naked mole-rats can be seen as counterexamples to the disposable soma theory of aging.
source: Nevertheless, both Fukomys and naked mole-rats can be seen as counterexamples to the disposable soma theory of aging, which assumes that the aging process is linked to an evolutionary tradeoff in which the preservation of the organism is essentially sacrificed to reproductive success (Kirkwood, 1977).
evidence: Inference based on the observation that breeders live longer despite reproductive costs, with citation to Kirkwood, 1977 for the theory

claim: 636 RNA-seq samples were analyzed covering 16 tissue types from both Fukomys species, sexes, and reproductive states.
source: Altogether, we performed RNA-seq for 636 tissue samples covering 16 tissue types from both species, sexes, and reproductive states (breeders and non-breeders).
evidence: Description of experimental design and sample size

claim: Each group (male/female breeders/non-breeders) of each Fukomys species consisted of 5-7 animals.
source: Each of the four groups (male/female breeders/non-breeders) of each species consisted of 5–7 animals (see Supplementary file 1a–e for sample sizes, animal data, and pairing schemes).
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: Species, tissue, and the combination of both variables accounted for 98.4% of the total variance in the data set.
source: Accordingly, a principal variance component analysis showed that species, tissue, and the combination of both variables accounted for 98.4% of the total variance in the data set
evidence: Supported by principal variance component analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: Individual differences explained 1.4% of the variance in the Fukomys transcriptome data set.
source: individual differences explained 1.4% of the variance, and only 0.004% was explained by breeder/non-breeder status (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by principal variance component analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: Breeder/non-breeder status explained only 0.004% of the variance in the Fukomys transcriptome data set.
source: individual differences explained 1.4% of the variance, and only 0.004% was explained by breeder/non-breeder status (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by principal variance component analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: Significant overlaps with the Digital Aging Atlas were found in three tissues: adrenal gland, ovary, and pituitary gland.
source: Across species and sexes, significant overlaps (false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.05, Fisher's exact test) with the DAA were found in three tissues: adrenal gland, ovary, and pituitary gland (FDR=0.005, each; Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3A

claim: The DEGs of the ovaries overlapped significantly with those from adrenal and pituitary glands.
source: Among these three endocrine tissues, the DEGs of the ovaries overlapped significantly with those from adrenal (p=2.8*10−27) and pituitary glands (p=0.005), but there was no significant overlap between the two glands (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3A

claim: The direction of status-dependent DEG regulation in Fukomys was significantly more often the same as in naked mole-rats (60% in females, 62% in males).
source: The direction of the status-dependent DEGs regulation in Fukomys, as found in this study, was significantly more often the same rather than opposite as in the naked mole-rat (females, 60%, p=5.2*10−58; males, 62%, p=10−44 for females, Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: Supported by comparison with Bens et al., 2018 data and shown in Figure 3B

claim: In guinea pigs, Fukomys reproductive status DEGs were significantly more often regulated in the opposite direction (57% in females, 59% in males).
source: In the guinea pig, on the contrary, the Fukomys reproductive status DEGs were significantly more often regulated in the opposite direction (females, 57%, p=9*10−25; males, 59%, p=4.7*10−23, Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: Supported by comparison with Bens et al., 2018 data and shown in Figure 3B

claim: Ribosomal protein expression was elevated in most tissues in breeders.
source: ribosomal protein expression (hsa03010 Ribosome, hsa03008 Ribosome biogenesis in eukaryotes, Figure 4A) was elevated in most tissues (and accordingly also in the weighted cross-tissue analysis).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: The strongest enrichment signal from MSigDB hallmarks came from MYC targets, which reflects enhanced ribosomal protein expression.
source: In MSigDB hallmarks, the strongest enrichment signal came from MYC targets (HALLMARK_MYC_TARGETS_V1), which can largely be considered a reflection of enhanced ribosomal protein expression and the fact that MYC is a basal transcription factor up-regulating genes involved in protein translation (Hofmann et al., 2015; Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4B and citation to Hofmann et al., 2015

claim: Expression of mitochondrial respiratory chain components increased in breeders.
source: In functional correspondence, we observed an increase in the expression of mitochondrial respiratory chain components (hsa00190 Oxidative phosphorylation, HALLMARK_OXIDATIVE_PHOSPHORYLATION, Figure 4A, B).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A and 4B

claim: Strong indications for increased protein degradation via the proteasome were found in breeders.
source: We also found strong indications for increased protein degradation (hsa03050 PROTEASOME, Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: The weighted cross-tissue proteasome signal was driven mainly by the adrenal gland and the gonads.
source: This weighted cross-tissue signal was, in contrast to the situation regarding ribosomes, driven mainly by two tissue types: the adrenal gland and the gonads.
evidence: Analysis of tissue-specific contributions to cross-tissue signal

claim: The expression of ribosomal genes was significantly linked to those of ribosome biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and proteasome.
source: We found that the expression of ribosomal genes (hsa03010) was significantly linked to those of ribosome biogenesis (hsa03008, FDR = 4.59*10−3), oxidative phosphorylation (hsa00190, FDR = 4.05*10−4), and proteasome (hsa03050, FDR = 4.59*10−3)
evidence: Supported by weighted gene co-expression network analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: Ribosome, proteasome, and oxidative phosphorylation pathways showed up-regulation of 3-9% on average in breeders.
source: Interestingly, ribosome, proteasome, and oxidative phosphorylation pathways also shared other characteristics of their differential expression signals: subtle fold-changes, that is, up-regulation of 3–9% on average.
evidence: Analysis of fold-changes in pathway expression

claim: The myogenesis hallmark was up-regulated in breeders, driven mainly by differential expression signals from muscle tissue.
source: The myogenesis hallmark (Figure 4B) was also found to be up-regulated in breeders. Expectedly, this weighted cross-tissue result was driven mainly by differential expression signals from muscle tissue
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: IGF1 was expressed most strongly in ovary and liver and was strongly up-regulated in the breeders' ovaries and adrenal glands.
source: This gene was found to be expressed most strongly in ovary and liver and was strongly up-regulated in the breeders' ovaries and adrenal glands (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Table 1

claim: IGF1 codes for a key regulator of anabolic effects such as cell proliferation, myogenesis, and protein synthesis.
source: IGF1 codes for a well-known key regulator of anabolic effects such as cell proliferation, myogenesis, and protein synthesis (Schiaffino and Mammucari, 2011; Jung and Suh, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Schiaffino and Mammucari, 2011 and Jung and Suh, 2014

claim: GH1 was strongly up-regulated in breeders in the pituitary gland.
source: Also, GH1 was strongly up-regulated in breeders in its known principal place of synthesis, the pituitary gland (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Table 1

claim: Xenobiotic metabolism was up-regulated in breeders.
source: With xenobiotic metabolism and TNF-α signaling, two defense hallmarks were also found to be up-regulated in breeders by the weighted cross-tissue analysis (HALLMARK_XENOBIOTIC_METABLISM and HALLMARK_TNFA_SIGNALING_VIA_NFKB, Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: TNF-α signaling was up-regulated in breeders.
source: With xenobiotic metabolism and TNF-α signaling, two defense hallmarks were also found to be up-regulated in breeders by the weighted cross-tissue analysis (HALLMARK_XENOBIOTIC_METABLISM and HALLMARK_TNFA_SIGNALING_VIA_NFKB, Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: The ROS hallmark comprising genes coding for proteins that detoxify ROS was up-regulated in breeders.
source: The up-regulation of the reactive oxygen species (ROS) hallmark comprising genes coding for proteins that detoxify ROS (HALLMARK_REACTIVE_OXYGEN_SPECIES_PATHWAY, Figure 4B) falls into a similar category.
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: Steroid hormone biosynthesis was significantly altered in breeders with both up- and down-regulated genes.
source: Another interesting aspect that was found to be significantly altered in breeders is steroid hormone biosynthesis (hsa00140 Steroid hormone biosynthesis, Figure 4A). In this case, both up- and down-regulated genes were in the pathway, and their absolute fold-changes were roughly balanced.
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: CYP11A1 was the most influential contributor to the differential steroid hormone biosynthesis pathway signal on the weighted cross-tissue level.
source: The most influential contributor to the differential pathway signal by far on the weighted cross-tissue level was CYP11A1, which codes for the (single) enzyme that converts cholesterol to pregnenolone.
evidence: Analysis of gene contributions to pathway signal

claim: CYP11A1 codes for the enzyme that converts cholesterol to pregnenolone, the first and rate-limiting step in steroid hormone synthesis.
source: The most influential contributor to the differential pathway signal by far on the weighted cross-tissue level was CYP11A1, which codes for the (single) enzyme that converts cholesterol to pregnenolone. This is the first and rate-limiting step in steroid hormone synthesis (Miller and Auchus, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miller and Auchus, 2011

claim: CYP11A1 was up-regulated in breeders in the gonads and the adrenal gland.
source: Because CYP11A1 was found to be up-regulated in breeders in its main places of synthesis – the gonads and the adrenal gland (Table 1)
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Table 1

claim: The total output of steroid hormone biosynthesis in breeders is increased.
source: it can be assumed that the total output of steroid hormone biosynthesis in breeders is increased.
evidence: Inference based on up-regulation of CYP11A1, the rate-limiting enzyme

claim: Sex steroids are produced at a higher rate in breeders, whereas circulating levels of glucocorticoids such as cortisol should be lower than in non-breeders.
source: The pattern of up- and down-regulation on the KEGG pathway, however, suggests that sex steroids especially are produced at a higher rate in breeders, whereas circulating levels of glucocorticoids – such as cortisol – should be lower than in non-breeders (Figure 4—figure supplement 4; see also our discussion on ACTH-R below).
evidence: Inference based on pathway analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: SULT2A1 is the main catalyzer of the sulfonation of DHEA to its non-active form DHEA-S.
source: SULT2A1 is the main catalyzer of the sulfonation of the steroid hormone dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) to its non-active form DHEA-S (Hammer et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hammer et al., 2005

claim: DHEA has repeatedly been proposed to be an 'anti-aging hormone' because its levels are negatively associated with chronological aging.
source: DHEA has repeatedly been proposed to be an 'anti-aging hormone' because its levels are negatively associated with chronological aging (Baulieu, 1996; Celec and Stárka, 2003; Rutkowski et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baulieu, 1996; Celec and Stárka, 2003; Rutkowski et al., 2014

claim: SULT2A1 is strongly down-regulated in breeders' liver.
source: We found that SULT2A1 is strongly down-regulated in breeders' liver, which is also the main location of its enzymatic action.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data

claim: MC2R encodes the ACTH receptor, which is the main inducer of glucocorticoid synthesis and a crucial component of the HPA axis.
source: The second candidate, MC2R, encodes the adrenocorticotropin hormone (ACTH) receptor, which is the main inducer of glucocorticoid synthesis and a crucial component of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis (Walker et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Walker et al., 2015

claim: Prolonged glucocorticoid excess leads to Cushing's syndrome in humans and many other mammals.
source: In humans and many other mammals, prolonged glucocorticoid excess leads to Cushing's syndrome.
evidence: General medical knowledge

claim: Cushing's syndrome patients exhibit considerably higher mortality rates.
source: The large overlap of these symptoms with those of aging could explain to some extent that Cushing's syndrome patients exhibit considerably higher mortality rates (Etxabe and Vazquez, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Etxabe and Vazquez, 1994

claim: The increased expression of the ACTH receptor in Fukomys non-breeders can cause similar expression patterns and consequences to Cushing's syndrome.
source: We hypothesized that the increased expression of the ACTH receptor in Fukomys non-breeders can cause similar expression patterns and consequences (Figure 5).
evidence: Hypothesis based on observed MC2R up-regulation in non-breeders and known effects of ACTH receptor activation

claim: Global fold-changes of the breeder/non-breeder comparison significantly correlated with those of a gene expression comparison of human controls/Cushing patients.
source: We subjected this hypothesis (Figure 5) to a first test by matching the global fold-changes of the breeder/non-breeder comparison with those of a gene expression comparison of human controls/Cushing patients (Hochberg et al., 2015) and found a significant correlation (R = 0.11, p=6.6*10−36).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis with data from Hochberg et al., 2015

claim: Cortisol levels are higher in hair samples from non-breeding F. mechowii than in those from breeders.
source: Altered MC2R expression (Figure 6A) coincides with higher cortisol levels in hair samples from non-breeding F. mechowii than in those from breeders of the same species (Begall et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Begall et al., 2021 and shown in Figure 6A

claim: Direct target genes of the glucocorticoid receptor were significantly affected by differential expression at the weighted cross-tissue level.
source: We tested whether the expression of targets of the glucocorticoid receptor (NR3C1) was significantly altered throughout our data using two gene lists (Phuc Le et al., 2005): about 300 direct target genes of the receptor that were identified by chromatin immunoprecipitation (i) and about 1300 genes that were found to be differentially expressed depending on the presence or absence of exogenous glucocorticoid (ii). Both gene lists were found to be significantly affected by differential expression at the weighted cross-tissue level (i, p=0.001; ii, p<10−9)
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis using gene lists from Phuc Le et al., 2005

claim: Weight gain in non-breeders was on average twice as strong compared to the weight gain in breeders during the experiment.
source: In line with our hypothesis, we observed that the weight gain in non-breeders was, on average, twice as strong compared to the weight gain in breeders during the experiment (p=7.49*10−3, type II ANOVA, Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6B

claim: The vertebrae of breeders were slightly denser than those of age-matched non-breeders.
source: In addition, we found a subtle but significant influence of reproductive status on the density of the vertebrae: the vertebrae of breeders were slightly denser than those of age-matched non-breeders (p=0.03 for vertebra T12 only, and p=0.01 across all examined vertebrae L1, L2, and T12; ANOVA, Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6C

claim: The vast lifespan differences between Fukomys breeders and non-breeders are associated with only subtle global pattern shifts in transcript levels.
source: The vast lifespan differences between Fukomys breeders and non-breeders are, according to our RNA-seq data, associated with only subtle global pattern shifts in transcript levels.
evidence: Summary of transcriptome analysis results

claim: Changes in the gene expression of the endocrine system play an important role in sexual maturation and in aging and the development of aging-associated diseases.
source: Changes in the gene expression of the endocrine system are well known to play an important role both in sexual maturation and in aging and the development of aging-associated diseases, for example, diabetes and cardiovascular diseases (Tatar et al., 2003; Chahal and Drake, 2007; Jones and Boelaert, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tatar et al., 2003; Chahal and Drake, 2007; Jones and Boelaert, 2015

claim: DHEA levels decrease continuously during the human aging process to an extent that favors it as an aging biomarker.
source: DHEA levels decrease continuously during the human aging process to an extent that favors it as an aging biomarker (Maggio, 2007; Traish et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maggio, 2007 and Traish et al., 2011

claim: DHEA is not only described as an aging marker but also as a marker for clinically relevant glucocorticoid excess.
source: Interestingly, DHEA is not only described as an aging marker but also as a marker for clinically relevant glucocorticoid excess (Burkhardt et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Burkhardt et al., 2013

claim: The regulation of adrenal gland MC2R causes a considerable proportion of the overall observed expression patterns and of the lifespan extension in breeders.
source: Regarding corticosteroid synthesis, we hypothesize that the regulation of adrenal gland MC2R, coding for the ACTH receptor, causes a considerable proportion of the overall observed expression patterns and of the lifespan extension in breeders (Figure 5).
evidence: Hypothesis based on multiple lines of evidence including MC2R expression, cortisol levels, and downstream effects

claim: The expression of the ACTH polypeptide precursor gene (POMC) is unchanged between breeders and non-breeders.
source: We found that the expression of the ACTH polypeptide precursor gene (POMC) is unchanged.
evidence: Gene expression analysis result

claim: Only PRKAR1B was differentially regulated in the adrenal gland among genes known to be involved in the regulation of MC2R.
source: Of those genes known to be involved in the regulation of MC2R (Beuschlein et al., 2001; Lin et al., 2007), we found that only PRKAR1B was differentially regulated in the adrenal gland.
evidence: Gene expression analysis with reference to genes cited in Beuschlein et al., 2001 and Lin et al., 2007

claim: One of the clearest symptoms of Cushing's syndrome known in many animal species is an increase in body fat and consequent significant weight gain.
source: While the opportunities to pursue the hypothesis upstream of the ACTH receptor were limited with our data set, many of the predicted downstream effects (Figure 5) could be verified. One of the clearest symptoms of Cushing's syndrome known in many animal species is an increase in body fat and a consequent significant weight gain (Ferraù and Korbonits, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferraù and Korbonits, 2015

claim: Osteoporosis is a known complication associated with glucocorticoid excess.
source: Another known complication associated with glucocorticoid excess is osteoporosis (Lodish et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lodish et al., 2010

claim: The GH/IGF1 axis of the non-breeders is impaired, which is a well-known symptom of chronic glucocorticoid excess.
source: Directly from our gene expression analysis we know that the GH/IGF1 axis of the non-breeders is impaired, which is another well-known symptom of chronic glucocorticoid excess (Ferraù and Korbonits, 2015).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data and citation to Ferraù and Korbonits, 2015

claim: The known, experimentally determined NR3C1 target genes show a clear pattern of expression differences between breeders and non-breeders.
source: According to our hypothesis, the known, experimentally determined NR3C1 target genes (Phuc Le et al., 2005) should therefore show a clear pattern of expression differences between breeders and non-breeders. This was the case for both the 1300 indirect (p<10−9) and the 300 direct target genes (p=0.001).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis using gene lists from Phuc Le et al., 2005

claim: All single DEGs mentioned in the paper were confirmed by the combination of limma and voom as an alternative DEG detection method.
source: For further validation, we applied the combination of limma (Smyth, 2004) and voom (Law et al., 2014) as an alternative DEG detection method to DESeq2 to account for potential dispersion problems in our data. All single DEGs mentioned in the paper were confirmed by this validation.
evidence: Validation analysis using alternative methods

claim: Hair cortisol levels of non-breeders are on average about twice as high as those of breeders.
source: Nevertheless, a recent study confirmed one of the most important predictions of the hypothesis: hair cortisol levels of non-breeders are on average about twice as high as those of breeders.
evidence: Supported by reference to a recent study (Begall et al., 2021)

claim: A subgroup of non-breeders defined by social environmental factor (one or both parents had died) exhibited cortisol levels nearly as low as in breeders.
source: However, a subgroup of non-breeders, defined by social environmental factor (one or both parents had died), exhibited cortisol levels nearly as low as in breeders (Begall et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Begall et al., 2021

claim: The drop of cortisol levels in orphaned non-breeders is accompanied by a substantial drop of mortality rates in this subgroup approaching the values of breeders.
source: The drop of cortisol levels in orphaned non-breeders is accompanied by a substantial drop of mortality rates in this subgroup approaching the values of breeders (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by mortality rate analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Across status groups (breeders, orphaned non-breeders, and non-breeders from intact families) mortality rates are clearly correlated with long-term cortisol levels.
source: This means that across status groups (breeders, orphaned non-breeders, and non-breeders from intact families) mortality rates are clearly correlated with long-term cortisol levels.
evidence: Inference based on mortality and cortisol data across groups

claim: The presence of breeders causes distress in non-breeders, resulting in constantly activating the HPA axis and contributing to reduced life expectancy.
source: Taken together, all evidence suggests that the presence of breeders causes distress in non-breeders, resulting in constantly activating the HPA axis and contributing to reduced life expectancy.
evidence: Inference based on multiple lines of evidence including cortisol levels, mortality rates, and social context

claim: Down-regulation of coagulation factors was observed in breeders in the circulatory system.
source: In the circulatory system, represented by blood and spleen, down-regulation of coagulation factors was observed in breeders.
evidence: Gene expression analysis result

claim: Coagulation factors are known to be up-regulated during aging in humans, mice, rats, and even fish.
source: Because coagulation factors are known to be up-regulated during aging in humans mice, rats, and even fish, this can be interpreted as a sign of a more juvenile breeders' transcriptome (Ochi et al., 2016; Benayoun et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ochi et al., 2016 and Benayoun et al., 2019

claim: The activity of coagulation factors is associated with a higher risk of coronary heart disease.
source: Furthermore, the activity of coagulation factors is associated with a higher risk of coronary heart disease (Lowe and Rumley, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lowe and Rumley, 2014

claim: No obvious histopathological lesions were found in the hearts or other organs (spleen, kidney, liver, lung) of non-breeders.
source: However, we found no obvious histopathological lesions in the hearts or other organs (spleen, kidney, liver, lung) of non-breeders.
evidence: Histopathological examination result

claim: Increased TNF-α signaling often leads to the induction of apoptosis.
source: Increased TNF-α signaling often leads to the induction of apoptosis (Annibaldi and Meier, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Annibaldi and Meier, 2018

claim: Apoptosis and P53 signaling were up-regulated in breeders.
source: In line with this, we found that apoptosis and P53 signaling were also up-regulated in breeders.
evidence: Gene expression analysis result

claim: Apoptosis is considered an important anticancer mechanism.
source: Apoptosis is considered an important anticancer mechanism (Baig et al., 2016; Pistritto et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baig et al., 2016 and Pistritto et al., 2016

claim: Up-regulation of apoptosis and p53 signaling compensates for cancerogenic effects of anabolic alterations in breeders.
source: We hypothesize this to compensate cancerogenic effects of the anabolic alterations described above (especially the up-regulation of the GH/IGF1 axis).
evidence: Hypothesis based on observed expression patterns

claim: Breeders are as 'cancer-proof' as non-breeders despite their much longer lifespan.
source: In line with this, our more than 30 years' breeding history with several Fukomys species in Germany and the Czech Republic suggests that breeders are as 'cancer-proof' as non-breeders despite their much longer lifespan (own unpublished data and R. Šumbera, personal communication).
evidence: Based on unpublished observations from breeding colonies

claim: Protein synthesis consumes 30-40% of a cell's ATP budget.
source: In line with this finding and with the fact that protein synthesis consumes 30–40% of a cell's ATP budget (Hands et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hands et al., 2009

claim: The expression of proteasomal genes is significantly linked to the genes of ribosome biogenesis and oxidative phosphorylation, indicating coordinated regulation.
source: The fact that the expression of proteasomal genes is significantly linked to the genes of ribosome biogenesis and oxidative phosphorylation indicates that those processes influence, or even trigger, each other and hence are regulated in a coordinated manner in Fukomys mole-rats.
evidence: Inference based on WGCNA results showing significant connectivity

claim: mTOR is an important positive regulator of ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis.
source: An important positive regulator of ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis is mTOR (Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2013

claim: The inhibition of mTOR is one of the best-documented life-prolonging interventions from invertebrates to mammals.
source: At the same time, however, the inhibition of mTOR is one of the best-documented life-prolonging interventions from invertebrates to mammals (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by references in Table 2

claim: mTOR is not significantly altered in almost all Fukomys tissues, with the exception of the adrenal gland where it is significantly down-regulated in breeders.
source: Given these conflicting premises, we find mTOR in almost all Fukomys tissues as not significantly altered; the exception is the adrenal gland, where mTOR is significantly down-regulated in breeders.
evidence: Gene expression analysis result

claim: The results of differential expression of anabolic components such as the GH/IGF1 axis are surprising given current aging research paradigms.
source: The results of differential expression of anabolic components such as the GH/IGF1 axis are surprising.
evidence: Commentary on unexpected findings relative to established theories

claim: The expression and secretion of GH and IGF1 decline with age in humans and other mammals.
source: based on the well-known fact that the expression and secretion of GH and IGF1 decline with age in humans and other mammals (Bartke, 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bartke, 2019

claim: Rudman et al., 1990 administered synthetic GH to elderly subjects, reversing a number of aging-associated effects such as expansion of adipose mass.
source: Rudman et al., 1990 administered synthetic GH to elderly subjects in 1990, thereby reversing a number of aging-associated effects such as expansion of adipose mass.
evidence: Supported by reference to Rudman et al., 1990

claim: Today's aging research strongly assumes that the enhanced activity of the GH/IGF1 axis accelerates aging and that its suppression could extend lifespan even in humans.
source: Today's aging research, on the contrary, strongly assumes that the enhanced activity of the GH/IGF1 axis accelerates aging and that its suppression could extend lifespan even in humans (López-Otín et al., 2013; Longo et al., 2015; Pitt and Kaeberlein, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to López-Otín et al., 2013; Longo et al., 2015; Pitt and Kaeberlein, 2015

claim: From worms to mice, the impairment of the GH/IGF1 axis by genetic intervention consistently led to longer lifespans.
source: From worms to mice, the impairment of the GH/IGF1 axis by genetic intervention consistently led to longer lifespans (Table 2)
evidence: Supported by references in Table 2

claim: Up-regulation of Klotho, an IGF1 inhibitor, extended the mouse lifespan by as much as 30%.
source: for example, the up-regulation of Klotho – an IGF1 inhibitor – extended the mouse lifespan by as much as 30% (Kurosu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kurosu et al., 2005

claim: Impairment of the respiratory chain by rotenone resulted in prolongation of the killifish lifespan by 15%.
source: whereas the impairment of the respiratory chain by rotenone resulted in prolongation of the killifish lifespan by 15% (Baumgart et al., 2016; Table 2).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baumgart et al., 2016

claim: Massive up-regulation of anabolic key components accompanies a lifespan extension of approximately 100% in long-lived mammals.
source: Therefore, it is astonishing that massive up-regulation of these anabolic key components accompanies a lifespan extension of approximately 100% in long-lived mammals and potentially even contributes to it.
evidence: Summary of findings showing contradiction with short-lived species

claim: The negative impact of enhanced protein synthesis on lifespan is to a large extent caused by the accumulation of damaged or misfolded proteins.
source: For example, it is, widely assumed that the negative impact of enhanced protein synthesis on lifespan is to a large extent caused by the accumulation of damaged or misfolded proteins, which is also known to contribute to aging-associated neurodegenerative diseases (Hipkiss, 2007; Saez and Vilchez, 2014; Carmona and Michan, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hipkiss, 2007; Saez and Vilchez, 2014; Carmona and Michan, 2016

claim: Up-regulation of the proteasome is known to counteract the accumulation of damaged proteins by clearing them, leading to lifespan extension in worm and fly.
source: Up-regulation of the proteasome, as we observed in breeders in a weighted cross-tissue approach and especially in endocrine tissues, is known to counteract these effects by clearing damaged proteins, leading to lifespan extension in worm and fly (Saez and Vilchez, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saez and Vilchez, 2014

claim: Enhanced proteasome activity has been linked with higher longevity of the naked mole-rat compared to the laboratory mouse.
source: Enhanced proteasome activity has also been linked with higher longevity of the naked mole-rat compared to the laboratory mouse (Pérez et al., 2009; Rodriguez et al., 2012) and in comparative approaches across several mammalian lineages (Pride et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pérez et al., 2009; Rodriguez et al., 2012; and Pride et al., 2015

claim: The simultaneously high anabolic synthesis and catabolic degradation of proteins will lead to a higher protein turnover rate in breeders and reduced accumulation of damaged and misfolded proteins.
source: We hypothesize that the simultaneously high anabolic synthesis and catabolic degradation of proteins will lead to a higher protein turnover rate in breeders and, accompanied with that, a reduced accumulation of damaged and misfolded proteins.
evidence: Hypothesis based on observed expression patterns

claim: The mitochondrial respiratory chain is the main source of cellular ROS that can damage DNA, proteins, and other cellular components.
source: the mitochondrial respiratory chain is the main source of cellular ROS that can damage DNA, proteins, and other cellular components (Balaban et al., 2005; Starkov, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Balaban et al., 2005 and Starkov, 2008

claim: At least 25% of genes in the reactive oxygen hallmark code for typical antioxidant enzymes such as thioredoxin, superoxide dismutase, peroxiredoxin, or catalase that can detoxify ROS.
source: Unsurprisingly, at least 25% of these genes code for typical antioxidant enzymes such as thioredoxin, superoxide dismutase, peroxiredoxin, or catalase that can detoxify ROS.
evidence: Analysis of gene composition in the reactive oxygen hallmark

claim: The known cancer-promoting effects of an enhanced GH/IGF1 axis could be compensated for by up-regulation of apoptosis and p53 signaling.
source: Furthermore, the known cancer-promoting effects of an enhanced GH/IGF1 axis (Junnila et al., 2013) could, to some extent, be compensated for by up-regulation of apoptosis and p53 signaling because these are the major mechanisms of cancer suppression (Bieging et al., 2014).
evidence: Hypothesis based on known mechanisms, supported by citations to Junnila et al., 2013 and Bieging et al., 2014

claim: Potential lifespan-extending effects of moderate up-regulation of both the GH/IGF1 axis and ROS production can be viewed in the light of the hormesis hypothesis.
source: More generally, potential lifespan-extending effects of moderate up-regulation of both the GH/IGF1 axis and ROS production can also be viewed in the light of the hormesis hypothesis (Ristow, 2014), which postulates that mild stressors can induce overall beneficial adaptive stress responses.
evidence: Interpretation based on hormesis hypothesis, supported by citation to Ristow, 2014

claim: Higher resting metabolic rates were found in breeders compared to non-breeders in F. anselli.
source: In line with these arguments, we found higher resting metabolic rates in breeders compared to non-breeders in F. anselli (Schielke et al., 2017), a species closely related to F. micklemi.
evidence: Supported by citation to Schielke et al., 2017

claim: The transition from non-breeder to breeder takes place in adulthood when by far the largest portion of the growth process has already been completed.
source: A second point that could help to resolve this apparent contradiction concerns the time of intervention. The transition from non-breeder to breeder takes place in adulthood when by far the largest portion of the growth process has already been completed.
evidence: Description of the timing of status transition in Fukomys

claim: Late treatments with rapamycin prolong the life of mice almost as much as those that are started early.
source: However, there are some exceptions: for example, late treatments with rapamycin prolong the life of mice almost as much as those that are started early (Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2013

claim: It is under debate whether the up-regulation of translation and anabolic processes by the GH/IGF1 axis independently enhances growth and aging or enhances aging only secondarily as a consequence of accelerated growth.
source: Therefore, it is still under debate whether the up-regulation of translation and anabolic processes by the GH/IGF1 axis independently enhances growth and aging or enhances aging only secondarily as a consequence of accelerated growth (Bartke, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bartke, 2017

claim: The Fukomys results are an argument that the GH/IGF1 axis enhances aging only secondarily as a consequence of accelerated growth.
source: Our results are an argument for the latter.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that status change occurs after growth is complete

claim: Most insights into current aging research originate from very short-lived model organisms.
source: A third point is the question of the transferability of knowledge obtained in one species to other species. Most insights into current aging research originate from very short-lived model organisms (Table 2).
evidence: General statement about the state of aging research

claim: The observed effects of lifespan-prolonging interventions are by far the smallest in the model organisms with the relatively longest lifespans: mice and rats.
source: It is clear, on the other hand, that the observed effects of lifespan-prolonging interventions listed in Table 2 are by far the smallest in the model organisms with the relatively longest lifespans: mice and rats.
evidence: Observation based on data in Table 2

claim: Knockout or knockdown of IGF1R in worms can result in lifespan extensions of more than 500%.
source: For example, knockout or knockdown of IGF1R in worms that normally live only a few days can result in a lifespan extensions of more than 500% (Houthoofd et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Houthoofd et al., 2004

claim: For mice, IGF1R interventions only lead to an extension of the lifespan by about 25%.
source: For mice that have a maximum lifespan of 4 years (Tacutu et al., 2013), comparable interventions only lead to an extension of the lifespan by about 25% (Holzenberger et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tacutu et al., 2013 and Holzenberger et al., 2003

claim: The effect size of lifespan-extending interventions would diminish further in mole-rats or humans that can live more than 20 or 100 years, respectively.
source: It seems reasonable to hypothesize that the effect size of such interventions, regardless of their direction, would diminish further in mole-rats or humans that can live more than 20 or 100 years, respectively, especially if the magnitude of gene expression change is small as in the comparison of breeders and non-breeders.
evidence: Hypothesis based on observed trend across species lifespans

claim: Gene expression patterns caused by lifespan-extending intervention in Fukomys mole-rats may highlight differences in aging mechanisms between short-lived and long-lived species.
source: Therefore, it may also be possible that those gene expression patterns caused by our lifespan-extending intervention in Fukomys mole-rats highlight particularly the differences in aging mechanisms between short-lived and long-lived species.
evidence: Interpretation of findings in the context of species differences

claim: The down-regulation of the GH/IGF1 axis in non-breeders may be a by-product of the apparent up-regulation of the HPA axis in non-breeders.
source: As a fourth perspective, one could interpret the down-regulation of the GH/IGF1 axis in non-breeders as a by-product of the apparent up-regulation of the HPA axis in non-breeders, which may well be adaptive in itself.
evidence: Interpretation of observed expression patterns

claim: Non-breeding Fukomys mole-rats can maximize their inclusive fitness by either supporting their kin in their natal family or by founding a new family elsewhere.
source: In the wild, non-breeding Fukomys mole-rats can maximize their inclusive fitness by either supporting their kin in their natal family or by founding a new family elsewhere.
evidence: Evolutionary interpretation of Fukomys social behavior

claim: The shorter lives of non-breeders could be adaptive on the ultimate level if longevity were traded against some other fitness traits, such as competitiveness.
source: It has therefore been suggested that the shorter lives of non-breeders could be adaptive on the ultimate level if longevity were traded against some other fitness traits, such as competitiveness, to defend colonies against intruders or to enhance their chances for successful dispersal (Dammann and Burda, 2006).
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citation to Dammann and Burda, 2006

claim: A constitutively more activated HPA stress axis is expected to offer advantages for both family defense and dispersal.
source: A constitutively more activated HPA stress axis is expected to offer advantages for both family defense and dispersal but it carries the risk of status-specific aging symptoms, such as muscle weakness, lower GH/IGF1 axis activity, and lower bone density in the long run (Ferraù and Korbonits, 2015).
evidence: Hypothesis based on known effects of HPA activation, supported by citation to Ferraù and Korbonits, 2015

claim: The effect of HPA activation may become even more pronounced under laboratory conditions where grown non-breeders cannot decide to disperse even if they would like to.
source: This effect may become even more pronounced under laboratory conditions where grown non-breeders cannot decide to disperse even if they would like to.
evidence: Speculation about laboratory vs. wild conditions

claim: The down-regulation of the GH/IGF-axis may be adaptive in itself for non-breeders if it has the potential to protect them from further damage.
source: However, even the down-regulation of the GH/IGF-axis may be adaptive in itself for non-breeders if it has the potential to protect them from further damage.
evidence: Speculation about adaptive value of observed expression changes

claim: Decreasing activity of the GH/IGF1 axis correlates with chronological age in a wide range of mammals, including mice, rats, dogs, and humans.
source: Note that for today's conventional view that stronger activation of the GH/IGF1 axis accelerates aging (Table 2) it is generally challenging that decreasing activity is well documented to correlate with chronological age in a wide range of mammals, including mice, rats, dogs, and humans (Bartke, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bartke, 2019

claim: Decreasing activity of the GH/IGF1 axis correlates, under pathological conditions such as Cushing's syndrome, with many symptoms akin to aging.
source: Also, decreasing activity correlates, under pathological conditions such as Cushing's syndrome, with many symptoms akin to aging (Figure 5).
evidence: Observation based on known symptoms of Cushing's syndrome shown in Figure 5

claim: The GH/IGF1 axis may be adaptively down-regulated in aging organisms as a reaction to already accumulated aging-related symptoms so that additional damage can be avoided.
source: It has been suggested that one solution to this apparent contradiction may be that the GH/IGF1 axis is adaptively down-regulated in aging organisms as a reaction to already accumulated aging-related symptoms so that additional damage can be avoided (Berryman et al., 2008; Milman et al., 2016).
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citations to Berryman et al., 2008 and Milman et al., 2016

claim: Translation and oxidative phosphorylation were among the strongest differentially expressed molecular processes concerning breeding status and were also the most affected by positive selection in the phylogeny of African mole-rats.
source: It is striking that translation and oxidative phosphorylation were among the strongest differentially expressed molecular processes concerning the breeding status. Earlier, these processes were also reported to be the most affected by positive selection in the phylogeny of African mole-rats (Sahm et al., 2018b).
evidence: Comparison of current findings with previous evolutionary analysis, supported by citation to Sahm et al., 2018b

claim: IGF1 was one of 13 genes found to be under positive selection in the last common ancestor of the mole-rats.
source: Furthermore, IGF1 was one of 13 genes that were found to be under positive selection in the last common ancestor of the mole-rats.
evidence: Reference to previous evolutionary analysis

claim: The corresponding mechanisms (translation, oxidative phosphorylation, IGF1) may have been evolutionarily adapted to be less detrimental and make their up-regulation more compatible with a long lifespan.
source: This may indicate that the corresponding mechanisms were evolutionarily adapted to be less detrimental and make their up-regulation more compatible with a long lifespan.
evidence: Hypothesis based on positive selection findings
